<reason>Side B (PRO) won a close, well-matched debate. CON's central route was the burden attack: self-censorship harms are invisible and unmeasured, so PRO cannot prove "more serious." PRO answered this honestly in Rebuttal 2 (A1), noting neither side has frequency data and resting the comparison on mechanism and scope—conspicuous penalties for teaching contested material versus no penalty for quiet avoidance—which CON never dislodged. CON's best substantive move, the "conversion" argument (serious omission-harm collapses into an affirmable false claim, i.e., a content defect), was directly answered by PRO's closing: students infer meaning from what teachers select, so distortion by omission needs no explicit falsehood, and CON's "a gap sits lightly" rejoin was assertion, not argument. PRO also effectively turned CON's misinformation-persistence point (partial accounts install durable false beliefs too) and landed the synthesis that fear-driven silence both distorts understanding and weakens the classroom's corrective capacity. CON's rhetorical edge ("That is not a ranking; it is a hope") kept the burden pressure live, but two of CON's speeches were clipped for word-limit violations—a real execution cost—while PRO's turns were clean and both PRO pressure questions were answered directly with A1/A2 structure.</best_rebuttal>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 2 move that PRO's voting-rights omission example "converts" into a content defect was the sharpest strike of the debate, but PRO's closing response—that students infer a misleading narrative from selective teaching without any explicit false claim, and that a syllabus can satisfy a topic requirement while concealing a thin treatment—neutralized it and preserved the invisibility-to-review asymmetry PRO needed.</best_rebuttal>
